quick: Opioid dependence: 12-16 mg/day SL (range 4-24 mg); induction per protocol
Allow sublingual tablet to dissolve fully; do not chew/swallow
May cause neonatal opioid withdrawal; use if benefit justifies risk
Present in milk; weigh benefit vs neonatal risk
No specific adjustment; caution in severe impairment
Reduce dose; avoid/caution in severe impairment

summary: Buprenorphine is a partial mu-opioid agonist used for opioid use disorder and for pain. It has a ceiling on respiratory depression but, combined with benzodiazepines/CNS depressants or alcohol, can cause fatal respiratory depression. Habit forming: Yes - it is a Schedule III controlled substance. It carries the opioid class boxed warning for addiction, abuse, misuse, life-threatening respiratory depression and neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome.
indications: Treatment of opioid dependence/opioid use disorder (sublingual tablet preferred for induction)
Maintenance treatment of opioid use disorder as part of a complete treatment plan including counseling and psychosocial support
Management of pain severe enough to require an opioid analgesic where alternatives are inadequate (transdermal/buccal/injectable formulations)

dosage.d: Begin 2-4 mg SL when objective withdrawal signs appear; titrate in 2-4 mg increments
dosage.n: Induce only with clear withdrawal to avoid precipitated withdrawal

dosage.d: Target 12-16 mg/day SL once daily (range 4-24 mg/day)
Start 5 mcg/hr patch; titrate every 72 h (or per product)

dosage.n: Avoid or use lowest dose in severe impairment

admin: Place sublingual tablet under the tongue and allow it to dissolve completely; do not cut, chew or swallow whole
If more than one tablet, place all under the tongue at the same time or in two doses, allowing each to dissolve
Begin induction only when objective and clear signs of opioid withdrawal are evident to avoid precipitated withdrawal
Strongly consider co-prescribing naloxone for overdose rescue
Taper gradually when discontinuing to avoid withdrawal
moa: Buprenorphine is a partial agonist at the mu-opioid receptor and an antagonist at the kappa-opioid receptor. Its high receptor affinity and slow dissociation produce prolonged effects and a ceiling on respiratory depression and euphoria, while displacing and blocking full agonists. This reduces opioid craving and withdrawal and provides analgesia.

absolute: Acute or severe bronchial asthma in unmonitored settings
Known or suspected gastrointestinal obstruction including paralytic ileus
relative: Concurrent benzodiazepines or other CNS depressants
Head injury or raised intracranial pressure
monitor: Signs of misuse, abuse and diversion

preg: Prolonged use during pregnancy can cause neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome, which may be life-threatening if unrecognized. Use only if the benefit justifies the risk; coordinate care for the neonate.
lact: Buprenorphine and its metabolite are present in human milk. Monitor breastfed infants for drowsiness, adequate weight gain, breathing difficulty and withdrawal; weigh benefits of breastfeeding against risk.
renal: No specific dosage adjustment is generally required for renal impairment, but use with caution in severe impairment and monitor for accumulation of metabolites.
hepatic: Buprenorphine is hepatically metabolized; reduce the dose in moderate impairment and use cautiously or avoid in severe hepatic impairment. Monitor liver function, as hepatitis and hepatic events have been reported.

major: Benzodiazepines and other CNS depressants - profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma and death
Alcohol - additive CNS/respiratory depression, potentially fatal
Other opioids/full agonists - may precipitate withdrawal or additive toxicity
MAO inhibitors - serotonin syndrome / opioid toxicity
moderate: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, ritonavir) - increased buprenorphine levels
Strong CYP3A4 inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine) - decreased levels/efficacy
QT-prolonging agents - additive QT effects (certain products)
minor: Naloxone (in combination products) - deters injection misuse
interactions.food: Sublingual absorption; food does not substantially affect SL/transdermal forms.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol; additive respiratory and CNS depression can be fatal.
interactions.diagnostics: May be detected on opioid drug screens; can elevate liver enzymes.

emergency: Life-threatening respiratory depression (especially with CNS depressants/alcohol)

monitoring: Respiratory rate and level of sedation, especially during initiation and dose changes
Signs of misuse, abuse, diversion and continued illicit use
Liver function tests at baseline and periodically
Withdrawal symptoms during induction and tapering
Pregnancy status and neonatal monitoring where applicable
counsel: This medicine is habit forming and is a controlled substance - take exactly as prescribed and do not share it
Never combine with alcohol, sedatives or benzodiazepines - this can stop your breathing
Let the tablet dissolve fully under the tongue; do not chew or swallow it
Keep naloxone available and tell household members how to use it
Do not stop suddenly; your doctor will taper the dose. Keep out of reach of children
pk: Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); keep secured from misuse/children
pearls: Habit forming: Yes - Schedule III controlled substance with potential for misuse, abuse and dependence
BOXED WARNING (opioid class): addiction, abuse and misuse; life-threatening respiratory depression; neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome; and fatal risk with benzodiazepines/CNS depressants
Partial agonist ceiling effect limits respiratory depression alone but not when combined with other depressants/alcohol
Induct only with objective withdrawal present to avoid precipitating withdrawal
Co-prescribe naloxone and combine with naloxone-containing products for maintenance to deter injection misuse
missed: For maintenance, take the missed dose as soon as remembered the same day; if it is almost the next day skip it and resume the schedule - do not double up. Contact the prescriber about any missed doses; do not take extra to make up.
overdose: Overdose causes pinpoint pupils, sedation and respiratory depression. Establish a patent airway and support ventilation. Naloxone may reverse respiratory depression but, owing to buprenorphine's high receptor affinity, higher or repeated/continuous naloxone doses and prolonged monitoring are often required. Call emergency services.
